text:
Dairy-Free Amaretto-Fudge Gelato

For the Gelato Base:
2 cans (13.5 oz each) full-fat coconut milk
½ cup raw cashews, soaked in water for 4 hours and drained
¾ cup granulated sugar
¼ cup light corn syrup
2 tablespoons cornstarch
¼ teaspoon fine sea salt
1 teaspoon vanilla bean paste or pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons amaretto liqueur

For the Fudge Ripple:
4 ounces bittersweet chocolate (70% cacao), finely chopped
½ cup full-fat coconut cream (scooped from top of chilled coconut milk can)
2 tablespoons amaretto liqueur
1 tablespoon light corn syrup
Pinch of fine sea salt

Begin by preparing your gelato base. Combine the soaked cashews and one can of coconut milk in a high-speed blender. Process on high for 2 to 3 minutes until completely smooth and creamy, with no visible cashew pieces remaining. This step is crucial for achieving the silky texture that mimics traditional dairy gelato, as the cashews provide richness and body that might otherwise come from egg yolks or heavy cream.

In a medium saucepan, whisk together the sugar, cornstarch, and salt. Gradually whisk in the remaining can of coconut milk until no lumps remain. Set the saucepan over medium heat and cook, stirring constantly with a heatproof spatula, until the mixture begins to steam and eventually thickens slightly, about 8 to 10 minutes. You are looking for a consistency that coats the back of a spoon and leaves a clean line when you run your finger through it.

Remove the saucepan from heat and whisk in the cashew mixture, followed by the vanilla and amaretto. The amaretto not only contributes its distinctive almond flavor but also helps lower the freezing point, resulting in a softer, more scoopable gelato. Strain the base through a fine-mesh sieve into a large bowl to ensure absolute smoothness. Cover the surface directly with plastic wrap to prevent a skin from forming, then refrigerate for at least 4 hours or preferably overnight. The base must be thoroughly chilled before churning to achieve proper aeration and texture.

While the base chills, prepare the fudge ripple. Place the chopped chocolate in a heatproof bowl. In a small saucepan, combine the coconut cream, amaretto, corn syrup, and salt. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat, stirring occasionally. Pour the hot cream mixture over the chocolate and let stand for 2 minutes without stirring. Then whisk until glossy and completely smooth. Let cool to room temperature, then transfer to a squeeze bottle or piping bag for easy drizzling. The fudge should be fluid but not runny when incorporated into the gelato.

When your base is thoroughly chilled, churn in an ice cream maker according to the manufacturer's instructions, typically 25 to 35 minutes. The gelato is ready when it has increased in volume and resembles soft-serve, holding its shape but still malleable.

Working quickly, spread one-third of the churned gelato into a freezer-safe container. Drizzle one-third of the fudge ripple over the surface, then use a knife or skewer to create decorative swirls. Do not overmix, as you want distinct ribbons of fudge rather than a uniformly chocolate gelato. Repeat with another third of the gelato and fudge, then finish with the final layer. Reserve a small amount of fudge for the top if desired.

Press plastic wrap directly onto the surface, seal the container with a tight-fitting lid, and freeze for at least 4 hours to firm up before serving. For the ideal gelato texture, let sit at room temperature for 5 to 10 minutes before scooping. The finished gelato keeps well for up to 2 weeks, though the texture is best within the first few days.

Serve in small bowls or cones, perhaps with a crisp amaretti cookie alongside for textural contrast. The intense almond notes from the amaretto complement the coconut base beautifully, while the bittersweet fudge provides decadent pockets of chocolate throughout each spoonful.

title: The Ultimate Barbecued Ribs
prompt: Write a recipe for "The Ultimate Barbecued Ribs". Write about 550 words. Output only the text itself, without any commentary.
text:
The Ultimate Barbecued Ribs

Select two full racks of Saint Louis–style pork ribs, each weighing approximately two and a half to three pounds. The meat should display even marbling with a rosy pink color, and the membrane on the bone side must be intact for proper removal.

Begin eight to twenty-four hours before cooking by preparing the dry rub. Combine one-third cup dark brown sugar, two tablespoons smoked paprika, one tablespoon kosher salt, one tablespoon freshly cracked black pepper, one tablespoon garlic powder, one tablespoon onion powder, two teaspoons mustard powder, two teaspoons ground cumin, one teaspoon cayenne pepper, and one teaspoon celery seed. Whisk thoroughly to eliminate clumps.

Remove the membrane by sliding a butter knife beneath the silver skin covering the bone side of each rack. Loosen enough to grip with a paper towel, then peel away in one firm motion. Pat the ribs completely dry with additional paper towels. Apply the dry rub generously across both surfaces, massaging into every crevice. Wrap each rack tightly in plastic wrap and refrigerate for at least eight hours, allowing the salt to penetrate deeply and the spices to anchor themselves to the meat.

Three hours before dinner, remove the ribs from refrigeration and unwrap them. Fire your charcoal grill using the two-zone method, banking all coals to one side. Add three fist-sized chunks of hickory or oak to the hot coals. Stabilize the temperature at 225 degrees Fahrenheit on the cool side, verified with a probe thermometer clipped to the grate. Place an aluminum drip pan filled with one cup apple juice beneath where the ribs will rest.

Position the racks bone-side down on the cool zone, running parallel to the flame with slight curvature to promote even smoke circulation. Close the lid with vents positioned to draw smoke across the meat before escaping. Maintain temperature between 225 and 250 degrees for the duration.

After two hours, the exterior should have developed a deep mahogany bark. Remove the ribs and lay each rack on a large sheet of heavy-duty aluminum foil. Drizzle one-quarter cup honey along the top of each, followed by two tablespoons unsalted butter cut into small pieces. Tightly crimp the foil to seal completely, then return to the grill, still bone-side down, for ninety minutes. This step gently braises the connective tissue, rendering fat and transforming collagen into succulent gelatin.

Combine the barbecue sauce while waiting. Simmer one and one-half cups ketchup, one-third cup molasses, one-third cup apple cider vinegar, one-quarter cup dark brown sugar, two tablespoons Worcestershire sauce, two tablespoons yellow mustard, one tablespoon liquid smoke, one teaspoon black pepper, and one-half teaspoon cayenne in a saucepan over medium heat. Reduce until thick enough to coat the back of a spoon, approximately fifteen minutes. Set aside one-third of this sauce for serving; the remainder will glaze the meat.

After the foiled phase, carefully open the packets—escaping steam will be intensely hot—and transfer the ribs back to the grill, still on the cool zone. Brush with the prepared sauce and close the lid for twenty minutes. Repeat with another layer of sauce, then continue cooking until the meat achieves your preferred tackiness, approximately thirty to forty minutes total in this final stage.

Test for doneness by lifting one rack from the center with tongs; properly cooked ribs will bow gracefully without cracking or falling apart. Alternatively, a probe thermometer should slide through the meat between the bones with minimal resistance, meeting something like softened butter.

Rest the finished ribs on a cutting board, lightly tented with foil, for ten minutes. This redistribution of juices preserves moisture when slicing. Separate by cutting cleanly between bones with a sharp chef's knife. Serve with the reserved sauce warmed on the side, coleslaw, pickles, and white bread for the traditional experience.

The result yields bark with profound smoke penetration, a rosy smoke ring beneath the surface, meat that clings to the bone until bitten, and fat so completely rendered that each bite dissolves on the tongue.

title: Dead Poets Society

text:
Robin Williams delivers one of his most memorable performances in “Dead Poets Society,” a film that manages to feel both timeless and urgently relevant. Set in the staid, all‑male Welton Academy in 1959, the story follows an idealistic English teacher, John Keating (Williams), whose unconventional methods—standing on desks, urging his students to “seize the day,” and reviving a clandestine poetry club—ignite a quiet rebellion among a group of earnest but constrained adolescents. The movie’s power lies in the delicate balance it strikes between romantic idealism and the harsh realities of conformity, making it a resonant meditation on the role of art, education, and personal authenticity.

Ethan Hawke, as the shy and introspective Neil Perry, anchors the emotional core of the film. Hawke captures the vulnerability of a boy torn between his deep love for acting and the iron‑fisted expectations of his authoritarian father. His performance feels both earnest and heartbreaking, especially in the scenes where he finally must decide whether to obey his father’s command or surrender to his own passion. Similarly, the ensemble of supporting actors—including Robert Sean Leonard (Neil’s best friend, Todd), Josh Charles (the nervous yet charismatic Knox) and Dylan McDermott (the self‑assured Charlie)—creates a believable microcosm of teenage camaraderie. Their improvisational chemistry gives each character a distinct voice, allowing viewers to see different facets of Keating’s influence: some become more confident, others more reflective, and a few sadly retreat deeper into the safety of obedience.

Peter Weir’s direction is measured, never melodramatic, and he uses the austere, ivy‑covered walls of the academy to emphasize the stifling environment the boys inhabit. The cinematography, with its soft lighting and lingering close‑ups, underscores the tension between the external order of Welton and the internal chaos that Keating’s teachings stir. The use of muted colors for the school’s interiors, contrasted with the warm tones of the secret poetry sessions in the cave, visually reinforces the film’s central dichotomy: the cold rigidity of tradition versus the vibrant, messy humanity of self‑expression.

The script, penned by Tom Schulman, is peppered with quotable lines that have entered popular culture—“Carpe diem,” “We’re all pretty desperate for something to fill the empty places inside us”—yet these moments never feel forced. Instead, they arise organically from the characters’ earnest attempts to grapple with the meaning of their lives. The film explores the danger of suppressing creativity, as illustrated by the tragic climax when the administration turns against Keating in an effort to protect its reputation. The emotionally charged courtroom‑style scene, where the headmaster denounces “unconventional teaching methods,” feels like a critique of any institution that prioritizes conformity over critical thought.

What makes “Dead Poets Society” endure is its unflinching honesty about both the joys and the costs of rebellion. Keating’s final walk off the stage, his silent salute to the students who rise in his honor, is a poignant reminder that true influence often lives beyond a teacher’s tenure. The film doesn’t simply champion nonconformity for its own sake; it acknowledges that daring to be different can lead to both empowerment and devastation.

In retrospect, the film can feel somewhat nostalgic, especially given the shifts in educational discourse and the growing awareness of mental‑health challenges among adolescents. Yet its core message—that art and poetry can be a lifeline for those who feel unseen—remains potent. The ending, though bittersweet, invites viewers to consider the legacy we leave when we dare to inspire others to think, feel, and speak authentically.

Overall, “Dead Poets Society” is a beautifully crafted, emotionally resonant piece of cinema that uses a small boarding school as a microcosm for larger societal tensions. Robin Williams’s charismatic performance, supported by a strong ensemble cast, thoughtful direction, and a script that balances sentiment with substance, makes the film a compelling exploration of the transformative power of education. It reminds us that while institutions may try to smother dissent, the human spirit—when nourished by poetry, music, and fearless mentorship—will always find a way to rise.

title: Saboteur
prompt: Write the body of an IMDb review for the movie "Saboteur". Do not give it a title. Write about 550 words. Output only the text itself, without any commentary.
text:
Hitchcock’s “Saboteur” is a lean, high‑octane wartime thriller that feels both grounded in the era’s anxieties and surprisingly timeless in its execution. The premise is simple but effective: an innocent man, a canny architect named Barry Kane (Robert Montgomery), is framed for a murder he didn’t commit and forced on the run, all while a shadowy enemy organization plots sabotage on American soil. From the opening beat, the film spins a web of paranoia that keeps the audience’s attention, and Hitchcock’s deft hand ensures that the tension never flags, even as the narrative barrels toward its climactic showdown on the Statue of Liberty.

Montgomery delivers a solid performance as the every‑man hero thrust into extraordinary circumstances. He balances vulnerability with a quiet determination that makes his plight feel authentic rather than merely plot‑driven. The chemistry between Montgomery and Priscilla Lane, who plays his resourceful girlfriend Pat, is understated but effective; Lane’s Pat is far more than a damsel in distress—she’s proactive, quick‑thinking, and willing to jump into danger alongside Barry. Their partnership fuels much of the film’s emotional core, and their occasional banter provides brief, welcome breathers amid the relentless chase.

The supporting cast shines in their respective roles. Alan Hale Sr., as the grizzled trucker who helps the duo evade capture, delivers a rugged charm that heightens the film’s sense of a ragtag resistance forming against a faceless enemy. The antagonists, particularly the cold‑blooded Karl (Walt Anderson) and the menacing "Pete" (Albert Dekker), are suitably menacing without descending into caricature, a balance that many wartime movies of the era struggle to achieve. Hitchcock also employs memorable cameos—most notably a brief appearance by a nervous telegraph operator delivering a critical clue—that add texture to the world he builds.

Stylistically, “Saboteur” showcases Hitchcock’s signature command of suspense and visual storytelling. The title sequence, a simple black‑and‑white opening with stark, angular type, sets a foreboding tone that carries through the film’s chiaroscuro lighting and stark compositions. The chase sequences are particularly noteworthy; the motor‑truck pursuit across the desert and the frantic subway chase use rapid cuts and tight framing to convey urgency without relying on elaborate special effects. The climactic face‑off atop the Statue of Liberty is both a literal and metaphorical summit, framing the conflict against an iconic American symbol that underscores the film’s war‑time propaganda undertones while also providing a breathtaking visual payoff.

The screenplay, written by Alan Le May and Martin Rackin, balances exposition with action. Hitchcock senses the need to explain the saboteur network’s motives without bogging the narrative down, and he accomplishes this through concise dialogue and effective visual cues. The pacing is brisk; at just under ninety minutes, the film never lingers, and each scene propels the story forward. That efficiency, however, sometimes sacrifices deeper character development—Barry’s backstory remains largely unexplored, and the enemy organization feels more an abstraction than a fully realized threat. Yet these shortcuts serve the film’s primary aim: to keep viewers on the edge of their seats.

Thematically, “Saboteur” operates on two levels. On the surface, it’s a patriotic call to vigilance, urging audiences to recognize the danger of clandestine enemies within. Beneath that, there’s a more nuanced meditation on trust, identity, and the fragility of reputation in a world where misinformation can turn ordinary citizens into fugitives. The film’s ending—where justice is restored, and the heroes emerge unscathed—might feel reassuringly tidy, but it also reflects the period’s desire for clear moral resolution amidst the chaos of global conflict.

In sum, “Saboteur” stands as an underrated gem in Hitchcock’s oeuvre, demonstrating his ability to craft a taut, urgent thriller that feels both anchored in its contemporary context and resonant today. Its crisp direction, competent performances, and relentless pacing make it a compelling watch for both classic film enthusiasts and newcomers seeking a brisk, suspenseful ride through wartime intrigue. If you’re looking for a concise, well‑executed thriller that balances action with Hitchcock’s signature tension, “Saboteur” delivers in spades.

The supporting cast, including Jodie Whittaker as Curtis's wife Annik and Kevin Godley as his manager Tony Wilson, add depth and nuance to the narrative, avoiding caricature and stereotype in favor of fully realized, three-dimensional characters.

Instead, Corbijn presents a candid and unsparing portrait of a young man struggling to cope with the pressures of fame, the constraints of his own personality, and the darkness that had long haunted him. The result is a film that feels both deeply personal and universally relatable, a powerful exploration of the human condition that lingers long after the credits roll.

The film's climax, which I won't spoil here, is both devastating and haunting, a heart-wrenching portrayal of Curtis's final days that feels both unflinchingly honest and profoundly respectful. Overall, "Control" is a masterpiece of contemporary biographical drama, a film that will resonate with music fans and non-fans alike. It's a must-see for anyone interested in the Joy Division story, but it's so much more than that – it's a profound and moving exploration of the human experience.

title: All the President's Men
prompt: Write the body of an IMDb review for the movie "All the President's Men". Do not give it a title. Write about 380 words. Output only the text itself, without any commentary.
text:
The film's portrayal of the Watergate scandal is meticulously researched and accurately depicted, thanks to the tireless efforts of the film's director, Alan J. Pakula, and its screenwriter, Mark Weinstein. The movie's attention to detail is impressive, from the smallest nuances of investigative reporting to the grand machinations of the Nixon administration. The film's commitment to accuracy lends it an air of authenticity, making the events that unfold on screen all the more disturbing and believable.

At the heart of the film are the performances of Robert Redford and Dustin Hoffman as Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein, the two Washington Post journalists who doggedly pursued the story despite the obstacles thrown in their path. Redford and Hoffman's on-screen chemistry is undeniable, and their characters' growing obsession with the story is deeply compelling. The supporting cast, which includes G. D. Spradlin as Mark Felt, Hal Holbrook as Ben Bradlee, and Diane Ladd as Sally Field's character's mother, adds depth and nuance to the film.

One of the most striking aspects of the film is its depiction of the bravery and tenacity of Woodward and Bernstein. The duo faced intense pressure and intimidation from the Nixon administration, but they refused to back down, even when the story seemed too big and too complex to tackle. Their determination and perseverance are inspiring, and their reporting helped bring about a constitutional crisis that ultimately led to the downfall of a president.

Pakula's direction is masterful, using a muted color palette and a deliberate pace to create a sense of unease and foreboding. The film's cinematography, handled by Gordon Willis, is equally impressive, capturing the drab, grey landscape of Washington, D.C. in the early 1970s. The score, composed by Lalo Schifrin, adds to the film's sense of tension and unease, perfectly capturing the mood of a nation in crisis.

Overall, "All the President's Men" is a gripping and thought-provoking film that holds up remarkably well even today. Its portrayal of investigative reporting is inspiring, and its depiction of the darker aspects of American politics is both disturbing and cautionary. The film's themes of accountability, transparency, and the importance of a free press are just as relevant now as they were when the film was released in 1976.

title: A Nightmare on Elm Street
prompt: Write the body of an IMDb review for the movie "A Nightmare on Elm Street". Do not give it a title. Write about 550 words. Output only the text itself, without any commentary.
text:
"A Nightmare on Elm Street" is a film that has left an indelible mark on the horror genre, and it's easy to see why. Directed by Wes Craven, this 1984 classic introduces one of the most iconic and terrifying villains in cinema history, Freddie Krueger.

The story revolves around a group of teenagers in Springfield, Ohio, who are haunted by Freddy Krueger, a disfigured killer with a bladed glove, in their dreams. The premise itself is chilling—the idea that a monster can enter your dreams and kill you is nightmarish in the most literal sense. This film taps into primal fears and the vulnerability of sleep, making it a standout in the annals of horror.

What sets "A Nightmare on Elm Street" apart is its innovative approach to the horror genre. Wes Craven masterfully blends psychological terror with gory practical effects, creating a experience that is both unsettling and visceral. The dream sequences are particularly noteworthy, with their surreal imagery and eerie atmosphere. Freddy's ability to manipulate the rules of dream logic adds a layer of unpredictability that keeps the audience on edge.

Robert Englund's performance as Freddy Krueger is nothing short of legendary. His portrayal of the child-murdering boogeyman is both terrifying and darkly humorous, a testament to Englund's acting chops. Freddy's distinctive appearance—complete with a fedora, striped sweater, and that now-iconic bladed glove—has become a staple of horror cinema. The visceral and grotesque violence is unflinching and jarring, effectively conveying the sheer inescapability of the nightmare, adding a new layer of relentlessness.

The ensemble cast, particularly Heather Langenkamp as Nancy Thompson, delivers compelling performances. Langenkamp's portrayal of a determined and resourceful young woman fighting to stay alive is both empowering and relatable. Her character's struggles to stay awake and outsmart Freddy are a testament to the film's themes of resilience and survival. The supporting cast, including Amanda Wyss and Rodney Eastman, also shine, adding depth to the story.

The film's pacing is excellent, balancing tension-building moments with brutal jumpscares. The soundtrack, by Charles Bernstein, perfectly complements the on-screen action, enhancing the eerie atmosphere. The practical effects, though simple by today's standards, are effective and gruesome, particularly the iconic "pullback" scene where Freddy's victims are dragged down into their beds by an unseen force.

One of the film's strengths is its exploration of parental guilt and the consequences of violence. The parents' past actions and their reluctance to confront them add a layer of depth to the story. This thematic complexity elevates "A Nightmare on Elm Street" above many of its contemporaries, making it a horror film with substance.

In conclusion, "A Nightmare on Elm Street" is a classic that continues to resonate with horror fans. Its unique premise, innovative filmmaking, and unforgettable villain make it a must-watch for anyone interested in the genre. The film's impact on pop culture is undeniable, and it remains a shining example of how horror can be both terrifying and thought-provoking. Whether you're a seasoned horror aficionado or a newcomer to the genre, this film is an essential viewing experience. It's a timeless masterpiece that has inspired countless imitations but remains unmatched in its originality and sheer terror.

title: Aliens
prompt: Write the body of an IMDb review for the movie "Aliens". Do not give it a title. Write about 550 words. Output only the text itself, without any commentary.
text:
"Aliens" is a masterclass in cinematic action and storytelling, proving that the sequel can often outshine the original. Director James Cameron takes the creepy sci-fi horror of Ridley Scott’s "Alien" and transforms it into a heart-pounding, adrenaline-fueled thriller that keeps you on the edge of your seat from start to finish.

Sigourney Weaver delivers a tour de force performance as Ellen Ripley, whose transformation from a reluctant survivor to a hardened warrior is one of the most compelling arcs in film history. Ripley's emotional journey is palpable, as she grapples with the horrors of her past and the looming threat of the alien menace. Weaver’s physicality and intensity make Ripley a believable and relatable heroine, despite the fantastical setting.

The cast is impeccably assembled, with strong supporting performances from Michael Biehn as Corporal Hicks, Bill Paxton as Private Hudson, and Lance Henriksen as Bishop. Each character is uniquely fleshed out, adding depth and authenticity to the assembled squad of Colonial Marines. The camaraderie and tension among the troops are masterfully depicted, making the stakes feel all the more real.

Visually, "Aliens" is a marvel. The sets, special effects, and lighting create an immersive world that feels both futuristic and grimy, a stark contrast to the pristine spaceship in the original film. The alien creatures themselves are even more terrifying in this installment, their design and movements enhanced by practical effects and sheer ingenuity. The famous "chestburster" scene from the first film is eclipsed by the sheer scale and ferocity of the alien hive and its inhabitants.

Cameron’s direction is precise and captivating, balancing high-stakes action sequences with moments of quiet tension. The film’s pacing is flawless, keeping the audience engaged without ever feeling rushed or overly chaotic. Key scenes, such as the covert infiltration of the alien hive and the climactic showdown in the Concentrator, are choreographed with mastery, ensuring that every shot and action is meaningful.

The soundtrack, composed by James Horner, perfectly complements the on-screen action. From the haunting melodies that underscore the film’s quieter moments to the thunderous percussion that accompanies the intense battles, the music enhances the emotional impact of each scene. The use of synthesizers and traditional instruments creates a rich, immersive auditory experience that adds another layer of depth to the film.

"Aliens" is not just an action movie; it’s a character study, a nightmare brought to life, and a testament to the power of storytelling. It raises important questions about motherhood, survival, and the human spirit, all while delivering thrills and chills in spades. The film’s themes of familial bonds and the fight for survival against overwhelming odds make it a deeply resonant experience.

In conclusion, "Aliens" is a cinematic achievement that stands the test of time. It blends intense action, compelling characters, and thoughtful storytelling into a seamless, unforgettable experience. Whether you’re a fan of sci-fi, horror, or just great cinema, this film is a must-watch. From the opening scene to the iconic final shot, "Aliens" leaves an indelible mark on the genre and on viewers’ memories. It’s a testament to the power of filmmaking and the enduring appeal of a good story well-told.

title: Goldsmith: 'I was not leant on'
prompt: Write the body of a BBC news article titled "Goldsmith: 'I was not leant on'". Do not repeat the title. Write about 550 words. Output only the text itself, without any commentary.
text:
The former attorney general Lord Goldsmith has told the Iraq inquiry he was not "leant on" by Downing Street to alter his legal advice on the war.

Giving evidence to the Chilcot Inquiry, Lord Goldsmith insisted his view that military action was lawful had not changed as a result of pressure from Tony Blair or his officials.

But he acknowledged his position had "evolved" in the weeks before the 2003 invasion, as he grew more confident in the negotiating history behind UN Resolution 1441.

Critics have suggested the peer was persuaded to harden his advice after initially warning that a second UN resolution might be needed to make an invasion legal.

Lord Goldsmith told the inquiry: "I was not leant on. I want to make that absolutely clear."

He said he had "agonised" over the issue but had come to his final view "on the basis of the legal analysis" available to him.

His original advice, drawn up in January 2003, warned that the safest legal course would be to secure a second UN resolution authorising force.

But by 17 March 2003, three days before the invasion began, he had concluded that the existing resolution was sufficient, allowing the US and UK to rely on the revival of earlier authorisations from 1990 and 1991.

Lord Goldsmith said a key factor had been the work of Sir Jeremy Greenstock, then Britain's ambassador to the UN, who had sought assurances from members of the Security Council about how Resolution 1441 had been negotiated and what it meant.

"That gave me confidence that I could conclude, as I did, that there was a firm basis in international law," he said.

The inquiry also heard about a series of meetings Lord Goldsmith held in Downing Street in early March 2003, including with Baroness Morgan, the prime minister's director of government relations, and Lord Falconer.

Lord Goldsmith accepted these meetings had taken place but denied they amounted to improper pressure, describing them as discussions about the process of finalising his advice.

The peer faced questions over why his full earlier reservations were not shared with the Cabinet, which heard his final position but was not shown the original written advice.

He said it was "a matter of regret" that concerns he had raised had not been communicated to ministers at the time, but he defended his decision to present an unqualified view in his final advice.

"You cannot have a situation where the attorney general gives a view to government which is equivocal," he said.

"Government has to know where it stands and the armed forces have to know where they stand."

Earlier, the inquiry heard evidence from Sir Jeremy, who said the US had been "disturbed" by the UK's determination to seek a second resolution but had gone along with the effort for the sake of alliance unity.

Lord Goldsmith, who served as attorney general from 2001 to 2007, has always maintained the conflict was lawful under the "revival argument", under which Resolution 1441 reactivated the mandate for force first granted following Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

Families of some of the 179 British service personnel killed in Iraq have questioned whether the legal basis for the war was properly established, and have been pressing the inquiry to examine the drafting of the advice in detail.

Lord Goldsmith is expected to face further questions when he returns to give evidence to the inquiry at a later stage, alongside other senior figures from the former government, including Tony Blair himself.

The inquiry, chaired by Sir John Chilcot, is not expected to publish its findings until the end of the year at the earliest.

title: A Smugglers Song
prompt: Write the body of a poem titled "A Smugglers Song". Do not repeat the title. Write about 550 words. Output only the text itself, without any commentary.
text:
In the hush before dawn we gather, lanterns flickering like moths against the tide,  
Boots sunk in the sand, the tide’s breath cold upon our calves, the sea’s secret sigh  
We are the chorus of rusted rope and whispered maps, the quiet men who slip between  
The borders drawn on parchment, the lines that men in marble rooms ink with fear.  

Hear the low drumming of the oars, the rhythm of a heart that beats in time  
To gulls that wheel above with a silver cry, to the moon’s thin blade that cuts the foam,  
And every splash that scratches the hull is a syllable in our clandestine hymn,  
A note that carries cargo hidden deep: spices, fire, love, and the ancient coin.

We sing of the wind that knows the shortcuts, the hidden coves where love is sold,  
Of the tide that rolls like a patient liar, bringing in the night and swallowing the day,  
Of the eyes that watch from ruined towers, and the smiles we wear like cheap medals,  
Of the ledger of debts written in salt, each line a promise, each promise a pawn.

Our voices rise, rough as the rope we twist, smooth as the silk we tuck beneath our coats,  
We chant the names of merchants’ children, the quiet prayers of widows, the sharp laugh of a king’s lieutenant,  
We hum the old verses that trade winds taught us, verses that can melt iron gates,  
That make the watchmen’s eyes flutter like moths attracted to a candle’s flame.

Listen—there is a drum in the hull, a beat of secret heartbeats, a pulse of risk,  
A cadence that tells of the night’s surrender, of the sea’s breath inhaled and exhaled.  
We glide past the cliffs where the law’s lanterns glow, steered by stars that bleed into the horizon,  
Our compass points not north, but to the places where hope is bartered for a breath.

We whisper of the sunrise merchants, of silks that smell of jasmine and blood,  
Of amber jars that hold the sun, of wine that sings of distant hills, of timber that bears the scent of pine,  
We trade words like contraband, slipping them through cracked doors, in the pockets of strangers,  
Our verses become the wind that carries a secret from one ear to another.

The tide turns, the night pulls back its veil, and the shore sings its own lament,  
The seagulls cry a chorus of warning, the lighthouse sweeps its amber gaze across the waves,  
Yet we—still—fold our sails, we fold our songs into the stillness, we hide the melody beneath the bark,  
Our covenant is the silence after the last note, the echo that lingers in salty air.

When the last cargo is unloaded, when the gold is counted and the stories are sealed,  
We sit on the dunes, the sand cool as a lover’s sigh, and drink the bitter tea of the night,  
Our fingers trace the lines of our maps, the ink fading like a memory, the paths we walked,  
We hum again, softer now, a lullaby for the dark, a promise that the sea will always keep its secrets.

So let the world think us thieves, let the galleons roar, let the courts judge what they cannot see,  
For we are the verses that the ocean writes, the song that never ends, the whispered hymn of the unseen,  
And when the moon climbs high and the tide kisses the shore one more time, we will be there,  
Singing, always singing, the smuggler’s song that rides the wind, that rides the wave, that rides the heart.

title: Man on the Moon
prompt: Write the body of an IMDb review for the movie "Man on the Moon". Do not give it a title. Write about 550 words. Output only the text itself, without any commentary.
text:
Milosh Forman’s *Man on the Moon* is a film that exists in the volatile, beautiful, and often contradictory space between biography and character study. While many biopics fall into the trap of a chronological, "birth-to-death" assembly line, Forman opts for something far more rhythmic and chaotic, mirroring the very subject it seeks to capture: Andy Kaufman. It is a film that refuses to provide a definitive answer to the question of who Kaufman actually was, and in doing so, it achieves a level of truth that a more traditional documentary-style approach never could.

Jim Carrey delivers what is arguably the most disciplined and transformative performance of his career. For much of his filmography, Carrey’s brilliance lies in his kinetic, rubber-faced elasticity—a superhuman ability to manipulate his features for immediate comedic payoff. Here, he tempers that energy, channeling it into a much more unsettling, internalised performance. He captures Kaufman’s profound loneliness and his pathological need to blur the lines between performance and reality. Carrey doesn't just "play" Andy; he inhabits the specific, manic frequency that Andy operated on. There is a vulnerability in Carrey’s eyes during the quieter moments with Lynne Loxton (Lauren Holly) that provides the emotional anchor necessary to keep the film from drifting into pure eccentricity.

The film’s structure is intentionally disjointed, leaping between various eras of Kaufman’s career and his personal relationship with Loxton. This non-linear approach serves a purpose: it mimics the experience of watching Kaufman himself. To watch a Kaufman performance was to be unsure if you were witnessing a joke, a prank, or a genuine breakdown. By fragmenting the narrative, Forman forces the audience into that same state of uncertainty. We are never quite sure when the "character" ends and the "man" begins, which is perhaps the most honest way to portray a figure whose entire existence was predicated on the subversion of identity.

The supporting cast is equally stellar, with several actors playing heightened, almost caricatured versions of real-life figures, which adds to the surrealist atmosphere. The film captures the specific, gritty energy of the late 70s and early 80s comedy scene, but it avoids being a mere nostalgia trip. Instead, it uses that setting to explore the isolation of the artist. Kaufman is presented as a man who viewed the world as a stage, but once the curtain fell, he found himself in a vacuum of his own making.

If there is a criticism to be leveled, it is that the film occasionally struggles to find its tonal center. The shift from the high-concept absurdity of his comedy sketches to the tender, heartbreaking developments of his personal life can feel jarring. However, one could argue that this tonal whiplash is the point. Life, much like Kaufman’s art, is rarely a smooth transition from laughter to grief.

Ultimately, *Man on the Moon* is not just a movie about a comedian; it is a meditation on the masks we wear and the heavy cost of constant performance. It is a flawed, messy, and deeply empathetic portrait that understands that the most interesting thing about a person isn't their public persona, but the inscrutable mystery that remains when the lights go down.

title: Army of Darkness
prompt: Write the body of an IMDb review for the movie "Army of Darkness". Do not give it a title. Write about 550 words. Output only the text itself, without any commentary.
text:
Sam Raimi’s *Army of Darkness* is a glorious, blood-soaked, and unapologetically campy masterpiece of genre filmmaking that serves as the high-octane conclusion to the *Evil Dead* trilogy. While its predecessor, *Evil Dead II*, perfected the blend of slapstick comedy and visceral horror, *Army of Darkness* pivots toward something entirely different: a swashbuckling, medieval fantasy epic viewed through a fractured, Looney Tunes lens. It is a film that understands the inherent joy of absurdity, trading the claustrophobic dread of a cabin in the woods for the wide-open, chaotic battlefields of a distorted past.

At the heart of this madness is Bruce Campbell, who delivers what is arguably the definitive performance of his career as Ash Williams. By this stage in the trilogy, Ash has evolved from a terrified victim into a reluctant, chin-forward action hero. He is the quintessential "everyman" thrust into a world of sorcery and skeletons, armed with nothing but a chainsaw for a hand and a double-barreled shotgun. Campbell’s charisma is the engine that drives the entire production; his ability to pivot from deadpan sarcasm to over-the-top bravado allows the film to maintain its manic energy without ever losing its sense of character. He doesn't just play a hero; he plays a hero who is frequently confused, frustrated, and wildly out of his depth, which makes his eventual triumphs all the more entertaining.

Visually, the film is a feast of kinetic energy. Raimi’s signature "shaky cam" and inventive POV shots are in full effect, turning even the simplest movement into a frantic, sensory experience. The production design, despite its modest budget, manages to create a world that feels lived-in and textured, even if that world is populated by deadites with exaggerated, grotesque features. The practical effects are a standout, utilizing stop-motion animation, puppetry, and heavy prosthetic makeup to create a sense of tangible, tactile horror that CGI simply cannot replicate. There is a weight to the gore and a physicality to the combat that makes the film’s more ridiculous moments feel strangely grounded in their own internal logic.

The tonal shift from horror to adventure is handled with a playful touch. While some purists may miss the genuine tension of the original films, *Army of Darkness* succeeds because it leans fully into its identity as a cult comedy. It mocks the tropes of heroic fantasy even as it celebrates them. The dialogue is snappy, the pacing is relentless, and the musical score adds a sense of grandiosity that perfectly parodies the epic cinema of the era.

Ultimately, *Army of Darkness* is a film made with pure, unadulterated passion. It is a celebration of B-movie aesthetics and a testament to the idea that filmmaking can be, above all else, immensely fun. It doesn't ask for your intellectual respect; it asks for your undivided attention and your willingness to laugh at the absurdity of it all. For anyone who appreciates practical effects, physical comedy, or the sheer spectacle of a man fighting an army of the undead with a power tool, this film is an absolute essential. It is a loud, messy, and brilliant triumph of imagination.

title: Jarhead
prompt: Write the body of an IMDb review for the movie "Jarhead". Do not give it a title. Write about 550 words. Output only the text itself, without any commentary.
text:
Sam Mendes's "Jarhead" is not a war movie in the conventional sense. There are no storming of beaches, no firefights in dense jungles, no heroic last stands. Instead, it is a film about waiting—about the grinding, soul-eroding tedium of being a soldier trained for violence but denied the chance to use it. Based on Anthony Swofford's memoir, the film follows a Marine sniper unit through training and deployment to Saudi Arabia during the first Gulf War, and it is far more interested in what war does to the mind before combat ever begins.

Jake Gyllenhaal gives a committed performance as Swofford, a young man who joins the Marines almost by accident and finds himself shaped by a culture of aggression he barely understands. The supporting cast is uniformly strong: Peter Sarsgaard brings quiet intelligence to his role as the spotter and observer, Jamie Foxx is convincing as the stern staff sergeant, and Chris Cooper and Dennis Haysbert make the most of limited screen time. But the real star of the film is the atmosphere—the oppressive heat, the endless drills, the desert that stretches in every direction with nothing to break it.

Mendes and cinematographer Roger Deakins create some genuinely striking images: oil fields burning on the horizon, black rain falling on white uniforms, Marines trudging across dunes in gas masks. These moments have a dreamlike, almost hallucinatory quality that suits the film's psychological focus. The use of music is also memorable, from the ironic use of "Don't Worry, Be Happy" to the Marines' ritual viewing of "Apocalypse Now" as a kind of shared mythology.

Where the film falters somewhat is in its structure. The narrative drifts, which is clearly intentional, but it means the middle section can feel as aimless as the soldiers themselves. Some viewers will find the lack of conventional plot and payoff frustrating. The film also struggles to fully develop its supporting characters, and the tension between Swofford and his fellow Marines occasionally feels undercooked.

Yet the film's central idea lands with real force. These men are trained to kill, told they are warriors, and then sent to sit in the sand while history happens around them. The famous scene in which Swofford has an enemy in his crosshairs but cannot get permission to fire captures the film's thesis perfectly: the gap between training and reality, between expectation and experience. The "jarhead" is a vessel for aggression with nowhere to pour it, and that frustration becomes its own kind of damage.

"Jarhead" is uneven, slow, and deliberately anticlimactic, and it refuses to offer the catharsis audiences expect from war films. But that refusal is the point. It is a thoughtful, visually accomplished meditation on masculinity, boredom, and the psychological cost of preparing for a war you may never fight. It won't satisfy everyone, but it rewards patience and offers a perspective on the Gulf War that most films ignore.

title: The Revenant
prompt: Write the body of an IMDb review for the movie "The Revenant". Do not give it a title. Write about 550 words. Output only the text itself, without any commentary.
text:
Alejandro González Iñárritu's *The Revenant* is less a traditional survival thriller than a sensory assault, a brutal and often beautiful meditation on endurance, vengeance, and the thin line between man and beast. Loosely based on the life of frontiersman Hugh Glass, the film follows Leonardo DiCaprio's trapper through a frozen American wilderness after he is mauled by a grizzly bear and left for dead by his fellow men—most notably the ruthless John Fitzgerald, played with venomous conviction by Tom Hardy. What unfolds is a nearly wordless odyssey of suffering and determination, shot with staggering technical ambition by Emmanuel Lubezki, whose continuous, roving camera work creates an almost unbearable immediacy.

The film's greatest strength is its immersive craft. Lubezki's natural-light photography captures the frontier with an elemental grandeur: misted forests, rushing rivers, and snowbound plains feel at once majestic and hostile. The infamous bear attack sequence is a masterclass in visceral filmmaking—chaotic, terrifying, and painfully prolonged, it sets the tone for a world where violence is sudden and indifferent. Iñárritu's decision to shoot in remote locations with long, unbroken takes lends the proceedings a documentary-like authenticity, though at times the stylistic flourishes border on self-conscious artistry. There are moments when the camera's lingering gaze on suffering feels less like storytelling and more like spectacle.

DiCaprio's performance is the film's emotional anchor. Working with minimal dialogue, he communicates Glass's pain, grief, and stubborn will through physicality—crawling through mud, gnawing raw flesh, and staring into the void with haunted eyes. It is a committed, punishing turn, though one could argue the role demands more endurance than emotional range. Hardy provides a compelling counterpoint as the paranoid, survivalist Fitzgerald, whose pragmatic cruelty makes him a worthy antagonist. The supporting cast, including Domhnall Gleeson and Will Poulter, is solid, though the film's sparse dialogue and relentless forward momentum leave little room for character depth.

Where *The Revenant* falters is in its thematic reach. The screenplay, co-written by Iñárritu and Mark L. Smith, gestures toward grand ideas—man versus nature, the cyclical nature of violence, the possibility of redemption—but rarely explores them with nuance. Glass's recurring visions of his deceased wife feel like heavy-handed symbolism, and the film's treatment of Native American characters, while sympathetic, leans on familiar tropes of noble suffering. The revenge narrative, meanwhile, is straightforward to the point of predictability; the destination is never in doubt, only the grueling journey.

Yet that journey is the point, and on a purely cinematic level, *The Revenant* is often breathtaking. The sound design—howling winds, cracking ice, labored breathing—wraps around the viewer like a frozen shroud. The film's portrayal of the fur trade era is grimly convincing, a world of mud, blood, and casual brutality. At over two and a half hours, it occasionally drags, particularly in the middle stretch, but the cumulative impact is undeniable.

Ultimately, *The Revenant* is an experience to be endured as much as admired. It is a film of immense technical skill and genuine ambition, anchored by a fearless performance from its lead. But it is also cold—deliberately so—and its relentless grimness can feel exhausting rather than illuminating. Those seeking a profound statement on the human condition may find it shallow; those seeking a visceral, beautifully rendered plunge into the abyss will find much to respect, if not quite to love. It is a punishing, impressive work—a monument to suffering that lingers in the mind like a chill you cannot shake.

title: The Matrix
prompt: Write the body of an IMDb review for the movie "The Matrix". Do not give it a title. Write about 550 words. Output only the text itself, without any commentary.
text:
To say that "The Matrix" changed the trajectory of modern cinema is a profound understatement; it did not merely shift the genre, it shattered the very glass ceiling of what an action film could be, both visually and philosophically. When it premiered in 1999, the concept was so radical, so audacious, and so perfectly executed that it felt less like watching a movie and more like witnessing a cultural event. The Wachowskis took the dense, complex world of cyberpunk literature and philosophy and distilled it into a narrative that was simultaneously accessible and deeply challenging.

The visual language of the film is nothing short of revolutionary. The "bullet time" effect, which allowed the camera to move around a stationary character during an action sequence, wasn't just a cool trick for show; it redefined the grammar of action filmmaking. It slowed down the chaos, giving the audience time to appreciate the choreography and the gravity of the moment. Combined with the distinctive green-tinted digital rain that falls through the sky, creating a sense of unease and artificiality in the simulated world, the film created a visual aesthetic that has been mimicked but never truly replicated. The contrast between the drab, beige, corporate mundanity of the real world and the vibrant, high-contrast digital landscape is a masterclass in visual storytelling, reinforcing the thematic dichotomy between reality and illusion without needing a single line of dialogue.

However, a film is more than just its cinematography, and "The Matrix" is anchored by a screenplay that, while occasionally dense, is remarkably effective. The dialogue is sharp, witty, and laden with double meanings that reward repeated viewings. Laurence Fishburne’s portrayal of Morpheus is perhaps the standout performance of the entire cast. He embodies the enigmatic mentor figure with a gravitas that feels timeless, delivering his lines with a calm, almost hypnotic confidence that commands the screen. Keanu Reeves, in one of his most celebrated roles, brings a necessary earnestness and vulnerability to Neo. His physical transformation for the role was evident, but it was his emotional journey from confused hacker to savior that resonated. His performance is understated, allowing the character’s arc to speak for itself, and his chemistry with Carrie-Anne Moss’s Trinity provides a subtle but compelling romantic subtext that grounds the high-concept sci-fi elements in human emotion.

The film’s themes are deeply resonant, touching on free will, determinism, and the nature of reality. It draws heavily on Plato’s Allegory of the Cave and Nietzsche’s ideas, weaving them into a plot that feels like a video game brought to life. The idea that our perceived reality might be a construct is not just a plot device; it is a philosophical inquiry that forces the audience to question their own perceptions. In an age where virtual reality and artificial intelligence are becoming increasingly prevalent, "The Matrix" feels more relevant than ever. It anticipates the digital age with startling accuracy, exploring the implications of a world where human consciousness can be digitized and controlled.

Critics might argue that the third act suffers from a lack of character development, prioritizing spectacle over substance. While this is a valid point, it is a minor flaw in an otherwise monumental achievement. The film’s pacing is tight, the action sequences are meticulously choreographed, and the emotional beats land with significant force. The final scene, with Neo making his choice, is a moment of pure cinematic magic, encapsulating the film’s central theme of choosing one’s reality.

"The Matrix" is a masterpiece that defies easy categorization. It is a sci-fi epic, an action blockbuster, a philosophical treatise, and a cultural touchstone all rolled into one. Its influence on subsequent films, from "Inception" to "The Matrix" sequels, is immeasurable. It raised the bar for special effects, action choreography, and thematic depth, setting a standard that few films have managed to reach since. It is a film that rewards analysis, re-watching, and reflection. For anyone looking for a movie that engages both the mind and the senses, "The Matrix" remains an essential viewing experience, a landmark in film history that stands the test of time with enduring power and relevance.

title: Stripes
prompt: Write the body of an IMDb review for the movie "Stripes". Do not give it a title. Write about 550 words. Output only the text itself, without any commentary.
text:
In 1981, John Badham took a chaotic ensemble of A-list stars, tossed them into a series of ill-fitting military uniforms, and handed them a script that was essentially a blueprint for disaster. The result was *Stripes*, a film that remains a cultural touchstone for its sheer, unadulterated commitment to physical comedy. It is a movie that does not care about logic, subtlety, or even basic physics, yet it manages to be one of the most fun and energetic comedies of the decade. At its core, *Stripes* is a story about redemption, or at least the attempt to find it through the absurdity of basic training. Bill Murray’s character, Russell Ziskey, is a man stuck in his mid-thirties, a corporate slave who has been let go from his job and realizes he has wasted his prime years. His solution? Joining the Army. The film follows his platoon as they are subjected to the brutal, often humiliating training regimes of Major Worm (Harvey Korman) and the increasingly unhinged Captain Brubaker (John Candy).

The genius of *Stripes* lies in its refusal to take itself seriously. From the moment the recruits are stripped naked and forced to run to the bathroom at the top of a long flight of stairs, the movie establishes a tone that is relentlessly physical. The humor is derived from the contrast between the high-stakes environment of military service and the complete incompetence of the characters involved. It is a playground for physical gags, from the infamous scene where the recruits are forced to eat live insects to the elaborate prank war against the more disciplined Alpha Company. Each gag builds upon the last, creating a momentum that never lets up. The film is a rollercoaster of pratfalls, slapstick, and verbal sparring, all delivered with a energy that keeps the audience on the edge of their seats.

John Badham’s direction is a masterclass in pacing. He understands that comedy relies on timing, and he ensures that every joke is delivered with the right amount of space. The camera work is dynamic, often moving with the characters as they stumble through their obstacles. This sense of movement mirrors the frantic energy of the plot, which jumps from one training exercise to the next without any real breathing room. The score, composed by John Williams, adds to the sense of urgency, often using martial rhythms to underscore the comedic chaos. It is a rare film where the music feels like a character in its own right, driving the narrative forward with a relentless beat.

The performances are stellar, largely because the cast clearly had a great time. Bill Murray is in top form, bringing a sense of bewildered dignity to a character who is out of his depth. He plays Ziskey not as a joke, but as a man trying to find purpose, which adds a layer of pathos to the farce. Opposite him is Harold Ramis, who is often underestimated but shines here as the platoon’s de facto leader. Ramis brings a groundedness to the chaos, anchoring the ensemble with his deadpan reactions to the insanity around him. John Candy, in one of his early comedic roles, brings a physicality to Captain Brubaker that is both hilarious and intimidating. He is the embodiment of the film’s chaotic energy, a force of nature who refuses to be tamed.

The ensemble cast is a highlight, with each member bringing their own unique flavor to the platoon. The chemistry between the actors is palpable, and it is clear that they trusted each other to push the boundaries of their characters. This trust allows the film to take risks that might have otherwise fallen flat. The result is a movie that feels like a group of friends having the time of their lives, and it is impossible not to be swept up in their enthusiasm.

*Stripes* is not a subtle film. It is loud, it is messy, and it is often absurd. But it is also a celebration of camaraderie and the human spirit’s ability to find joy in the most unlikely of circumstances. It is a reminder that sometimes, the best way to deal with the absurdity of life is to lean into it. In the end, *Stripes* is a triumph of pure comedic energy, a film that knows exactly what it is and embraces it with open arms. It is a classic for a reason, and it remains as fun to watch today as it was when it first hit theaters. If you are looking for a film that will make you laugh, cry (with laughter), and feel like a kid again, *Stripes* is the perfect choice. It is a masterclass in ensemble comedy, a film that proves that sometimes, the most serious joke is the one that changes your life.

title: South Park: Bigger, Longer & Uncut
prompt: Write the body of an IMDb review for the movie "South Park: Bigger, Longer & Uncut". Do not give it a title. Write about 550 words. Output only the text itself, without any commentary.
text:
I first saw this movie in a theater the summer it came out, and I've been telling people ever since that it's one of the most underrated pieces of satire of the 1990s. Yes, it's crude. Yes, it's obscene. Yes, it probably has more curse words per minute than anything else ever committed to film. But it's also — and I say this without a hint of irony — a genuinely clever musical and one of the sharpest takedowns of censorship and moral panic ever made.

The premise is so simple it's brilliant: the boys sneak into the R-rated Terrance and Phillip movie, walk out spouting an exciting new vocabulary, and their parents respond by declaring war on Canada. That escalation — from a dirty movie to an actual war, complete with scheduled executions — sounds absurd, and it is, but that's the point. Parker and Stone understand that moral panic IS absurd. Every adult in the movie reacts to their children's behavior by blaming someone else, and the whole plot is built on that deflection. The parents blame Canada, the government blames Terrance and Phillip, and everybody scrambles to avoid the terrifying possibility of looking in a mirror. "Blame Canada" is hilarious on the surface, but the lyrics — "we must blame them and cause a fuss before somebody thinks of blaming us" — are a more honest summary of American political life than most serious films manage.

And the songs! I wasn't prepared for how good the music is. "Uncle F***a" is filthy in exactly the way a Broadway parody should be, but "It's Easy, Mmmkay" is a legitimately well-constructed number with rhymes that would make Sondheim smirk. "Up There," Satan's big ballad, is played completely straight — a yearning "I Want" song straight out of a Disney film — and it works because Parker and Stone genuinely know the conventions they're sending up. "Blame Canada" getting an Oscar nomination was the cherry on top: the Academy honoring a song whose entire thesis is scapegoating, with nobody catching the irony.

The subplot with Satan and Saddam Hussein still kills me. Satan as a lonely, sensitive soul trapped in an abusive relationship with Saddam shouldn't work, but the sincerity makes it weirdly touching, and it feeds into an ending that gives Kenny — the character who dies constantly — an actual emotional payoff. I never expected a South Park movie to make me feel something, and there I was in the theater, a little moved. Ridiculous, but true.

What impresses me most on rewatch is how tight it is. Barely eighty minutes, no fat, every joke and musical number serving the story. The animation is deliberately cheap, but the writing is anything but — gags come so fast and from so many directions (the V-chip, the MPAA jabs, the finale that's somehow both sincere and mocking) that the movie stays a step ahead of you the whole way.

The great irony, of course, is that a film arguing against censorship had to fight the ratings board tooth and nail to get released. But the argument holds up: the kids' real problem was never the swearing, it was the adults too busy pointing fingers to actually parent. That message predates and outlasts every outrage cycle since.

Crude on the surface, razor-sharp underneath. 10/10, and Uncle F***a forever.

title: In the Name of the Father
prompt: Write the body of an IMDb review for the movie "In the Name of the Father". Do not give it a title. Write about 550 words. Output only the text itself, without any commentary.
text:
Jim Sheridan's "In the Name of the Father" stands as one of the most powerful courtroom dramas ever committed to film, yet it transcends the genre entirely to become something far more devastating: a true story of institutional cruelty, familial bonds forged and tested under impossible circumstances, and the agonizingly slow machinery of justice. Based on the real-life case of Gerry Conlon and the Guildford Four, the film refuses the easy comforts of inspirational biopic conventions, instead immersing viewers in the suffocating nightmare of a justice system that has already decided your guilt before you enter the courtroom.

Daniel Day-Lewis delivers what might be his most physically and emotionally raw performance as Gerry Conlon, a petty Belfast thief whose life careens from minor criminal hijinks in 1970s London to becoming the centerpiece of one of Britain's most notorious miscarriages of justice. The early scenes establish Conlon as almost recklessly charming, a young man whose fundamental decency is obscured by his restlessness and poor judgment. Day-Lewis allows us to see the boy beneath the bluster, making his subsequent transformation all the more shattering. When Gerry and his friend Paul Hill are arrested for the Guildford pub bombings—IRA attacks they had nothing to do with—the film enters a darker register that it never truly abandons.

The interrogation sequences are masterpieces of escalating dread. Sheridan understands that the true horror lies not in obvious brutality but in the psychological dismantling of innocent people, the way confessions are extracted through sleep deprivation, intimidation, and the manipulation of fear. Pete Postlethwaite's Giuseppe Conlon, Gerry's father, enters this nightmare when he travels to London to help his son and finds himself ensnared in the same conspiracy. Postlethwaite's performance is the film's quiet miracle—his Giuseppe is a man of almost painful gentleness, a believer in systems and decency that fail him at every turn. The father-son dynamic that develops in prison contains the film's true emotional architecture. These are men who barely knew how to speak to each other in freedom, forced into proximity by concrete and steel, discovering too late the depth of their connection.

Emma Thompson enters the narrative as Gareth Peirce, the solicitor who eventually uncovers the suppressed evidence that proves the Conlons' innocence. Thompson wisely underplays, understanding that in a story this inherently dramatic, restraint becomes its own form of power. Her Peirce is exhausted, outraged, and tenacious—a professional who understands that her clients' lives depend on her refusal to accept convenient narratives.

What elevates "In the Name of the Father" beyond standard issue-issue cinema is Sheridan's refusal to simplify. The film acknowledges the real horror of the Guildford bombings without allowing that horror to justify the imprisonment of innocent people. It shows Gerry's genuine flaws while insisting that these flaws are irrelevant to the question of his guilt. Most painfully, it captures the way injustice compounds upon itself—the original crime of false conviction layered with the suppression of evidence, the denial of appeals, the bureaucratic indifference to ruined lives.

Trevor Jones's score, with its keening Irish instrumentation, and Peter Biziou's grainy cinematography create an atmosphere of sustained mournfulness. The film's final movement, as the truth finally emerges through Peirce's determination and a belated act of institutional conscience, offers not triumph but something more complicated—a sense of justice too delayed to be fully satisfying, of lives that cannot be fully restored.

"In the Name of the Father" remains essential viewing not merely as historical document but as ongoing warning. The systems it depicts have not been dismantled; they have evolved, adapted, found new targets. The film's final power lies in its implicit question, still unanswered: how many others remain imprisoned not by evidence but by the refusal of power to acknowledge its own errors?

title: Shakespeare in Love
prompt: Write the body of an IMDb review for the movie "Shakespeare in Love". Do not give it a title. Write about 550 words. Output only the text itself, without any commentary.
text:
Shakespeare in Love remains one of the most delightful cinematic achievements of the 1990s, a film that somehow manages to be both a loving homage to the Bard and a cheeky subversion of everything we think we know about him. John Madden's direction, paired with Marc Norman and Tom Stoppard's razor-sharp screenplay, creates a world where the boundaries between life and art dissolve with intoxicating joy.

What elevates this film beyond mere romantic comedy is its genuine passion for the creative process itself. We watch Shakespeare not as some untouchable literary deity, but as a struggling artist desperate for inspiration, blocked and broke in a theatrical landscape that feels remarkably recognizable. The film understands that creativity often emerges from constraint, from deadline pressure, from the messy collision of personal longing and professional ambition. When Will meets Viola de Lesseps, disguised as a boy to audition for his new play, the sparks that fly ignite both a secret romance and the greatest love story ever written.

Gwyneth Paltrow delivers the performance of her career as Viola, capturing both the fierce intelligence of a woman who refuses to accept the limitations placed upon her gender and the trembling vulnerability of someone experiencing first love. Her Viola is no passive muse but an active collaborator, feeding lines and ideas to her lover, becoming the very heartbeat of his work. You believe completely that this woman could inspire immortal poetry, that her courage in pursuing love against impossible odds might find permanent residence in verse.

Joseph Fiennes makes for a surprisingly earthy Shakespeare, all nervous energy and hungry eyes. He plays the playwright as a creature of pure appetite—for language, for recognition, for love. The scenes between him and Paltrow crackle with erotic tension and intellectual playfulness. Their first scene together, with Viola reciting his own words back to him without recognizing their author, sets the film's central theme in motion: art and life are inseparable, each feeding voraciously upon the other.

The supporting cast operates at the same extraordinary level. Judi Dench's brief appearance as Queen Elizabeth I won her a thoroughly deserved Oscar; she commands every frame she occupies with imperious wit and unexpected warmth. Geoffrey Rush's Philip Henslowe provides chaotic comic relief while somehow grounding the theatrical world in economic reality—he needs a hit, and he needs it now. Tom Wilkinson, Colin Firth, Ben Affleck, and the marvelous Jim Carter all contribute to a rich tapestry of Elizabethan London that feels lived-in rather than museum-piece pristine.

The film's visual pleasures are considerable. Richard Greatrex's cinematography bathes everything in golden candlelight and autumnal warmth, while Sandy Powell's costume design balances historical authenticity with cinematic flamboyance. The recreation of the Rose Theatre, and the sequence depicting the premiere of Romeo and Juliet, generate genuine excitement—we feel the nervy thrill of theatrical performance, the communion between players and audience that makes live drama irreplaceable.

Some critics have dismissed Shakespeare in Love as merely clever, accusing it of reducing great art to biographical incident. This seems to me a fundamental misreading. The film never claims to explain Shakespeare's genius; rather, it celebrates the mysterious alchemy by which personal experience transforms into something universal. We need not believe that Romeo and Juliet was actually written this way to appreciate the truth the film expresses about all artistic creation—that it emerges from the quarrel between private feeling and public form.

The ending, necessarily bittersweet, honors both the transcendent power of art and the human cost exacted in its service. Viola and Will cannot remain together, yet something of their love persists in every performance of his play, in every audience moved to tears by words written in the white heat of their impossible romance. Shakespeare in Love understands that this is not consolation enough, yet also that it is something—perhaps the only something we have against time and loss.

Twenty-five years later, the film retains its charm, its wit, and its surprising emotional depth. It reminds us why we fell in love with movies in the first place: the darkness, the collective breath held, the sudden, miraculous appearance of something beautiful where nothing existed before.

title: I don't fully understand so maybe someone help out...
