To the Editor,

The debate surrounding the impact of computers on our daily lives has become one of the most polarizing discussions of our time. On one hand, we are told that digital devices are the great equalizers, bridging geographical gaps and enhancing cognitive skills. On the other hand, critics argue that our screens are eroding our physical health, severing meaningful human connections, and disconnecting us from the natural world. While I acknowledge the profound risks associated with excessive screen time, I firmly believe that when used with intention and balance, computers serve as indispensable tools that enrich our lives, foster global empathy, and provide economic and educational opportunities that were previously unimaginable. We must not throw out the digital baby with the bathwater; instead, we must champion a healthier, more conscious relationship with technology.

First, consider the unprecedented access to knowledge and education that computers provide. In the past, learning was often limited by geography, economic status, or the availability of local institutions. Today, a student in a rural village can access the same lectures as a student at a prestigious university, and a working professional can upskill at midnight. This democratization of information is not merely a convenience; it is a fundamental shift in how society operates. It empowers individuals to pursue careers, hobbies, and self-improvement that were previously out of reach. Furthermore, the argument that computers harm hand-eye coordination is outdated. While static video games are often blamed, modern interactive software and virtual reality are actually being used in therapy to improve motor skills and cognitive flexibility. The digital realm is a gymnasium for the mind, offering puzzles, simulations, and complex problem-solving scenarios that keep our neural pathways active and adaptable.

Secondly, computers have revolutionized human connection, particularly for those who are isolated. For individuals with chronic illnesses, social anxiety, or those living in remote areas, online communities are not a substitute for face-to-face interaction; they are a lifeline. They provide a space where people can find belonging, share experiences, and receive support that might not be available in their immediate physical environment. While critics worry about "online friends" replacing real ones, we must recognize that friendship is not strictly defined by physical proximity. The ability to video call a relative across the ocean, to collaborate with colleagues in different time zones, or to join a global conversation about a shared passion creates a fabric of global empathy. We are becoming more aware of issues on the other side of the world, fostering a sense of shared humanity that was previously difficult to achieve.

However, I do not dismiss the valid concerns regarding sedentary lifestyles and the displacement of nature. It is true that excessive screen time can lead to physical inactivity and mental fatigue. But this is a problem of moderation and design, not an inherent flaw of the technology itself. The solution is not to ban computers, but to educate ourselves and our children on digital hygiene. We must advocate for workplaces that encourage standing desks and movement, for schools that integrate outdoor time, and for individuals who set boundaries for their own device usage. We can embrace the digital world without sacrificing the physical one.

In conclusion, computers are a neutral tool that amplifies whatever intent is behind them. They can isolate or connect, they can educate or distract. The choice lies in how we use them. Rather than fearing this technology, we should strive to master it. By establishing healthy boundaries and recognizing the immense potential for learning and connection, we can ensure that computers remain a force for good, enhancing our lives without diminishing our humanity. Let us not look back with regret, but forward with responsibility, harnessing the power of the digital age to build a more informed, connected, and equitable society.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Citizen

I have designed a schematic based on the typical daisy-chain configuration found in the MAX7219 datasheet and various online tutorials. My primary concern is signal integrity and potential power issues, as I am relatively new to interfacing with high-current display drivers. I would appreciate a review of the schematic to ensure I haven't overlooked any critical components or connections that could lead to device failure or erratic behavior.

The system is powered by a 5V USB supply. I used a 1117-5.0 linear regulator to generate a stable 5V rail for the logic and the MAX7219 modules, as the ESP32 can tolerate up to 3.6V on its GPIO pins, but the MAX7219 requires 5V for proper driving capability of the LEDs. I placed a 10uF tantalum capacitor and a 100nF ceramic capacitor at the input of the regulator, and a 10uF and 100nF combination at the output, close to the pin 1 (V+) of each MAX7219 module. I believe this should handle the transient current spikes when the displays update, but I am unsure if 10uF is sufficient for a 4-module chain. Some sources suggest using larger bulk capacitors, perhaps 100uF, near the last module in the chain to handle the cumulative inductive kickback from the LED segments. Should I add these, or is my current placement adequate?

Regarding the communication interface, I am using the standard 3-wire serial interface: DIN, CS, and CLK. I connected the CS line directly to GPIO 15 of the ESP32. Since the MAX7219 uses active-low chip select logic, I ensured the line is pulled high when not in use via an internal pull-up, though I also added a 10kΩ external pull-up resistor to VCC for stability. The DIN and CLK lines are connected to GPIO 16 and GPIO 17, respectively. I am aware that these GPIOs have internal pull-ups and pull-downs, but I have disabled them in the code to prevent any contention. I first saw this movie in a theater the summer it came out, and I've been telling people ever since that it's one of the most underrated pieces of satire of the 1990s. Yes, it's crude. Yes, it's obscene. Yes, it probably has more curse words per minute than anything else ever committed to film. But it's also — and I say this without a hint of irony — a genuinely clever musical and one of the sharpest takedowns of censorship and moral panic ever made.

The premise is so simple it's brilliant: the boys sneak into the R-rated Terrance and Phillip movie, walk out spouting an exciting new vocabulary, and their parents respond by declaring war on Canada. That escalation — from a dirty movie to an actual war, complete with scheduled executions — sounds absurd, and it is, but that's the point. Parker and Stone understand that moral panic IS absurd. Every adult in the movie reacts to their children's behavior by blaming someone else, and the whole plot is built on that deflection. The parents blame Canada, the government blames Terrance and Phillip, and everybody scrambles to avoid the terrifying possibility of looking in a mirror. "Blame Canada" is hilarious on the surface, but the lyrics — "we must blame them and cause a fuss before somebody thinks of blaming us" — are a more honest summary of American political life than most serious films manage.

And the songs! I wasn't prepared for how good the music is. "Uncle F***a" is filthy in exactly the way a Broadway parody should be, but "It's Easy, Mmmkay" is a legitimately well-constructed number with rhymes that would make Sondheim smirk. "Up There," Satan's big ballad, is played completely straight — a yearning "I Want" song straight out of a Disney film — and it works because Parker and Stone genuinely know the conventions they're sending up. "Blame Canada" getting an Oscar nomination was the cherry on top: the Academy honoring a song whose entire thesis is scapegoating, with nobody catching the irony.

The subplot with Satan and Saddam Hussein still kills me. Satan as a lonely, sensitive soul trapped in an abusive relationship with Saddam shouldn't work, but the sincerity makes it weirdly touching, and it feeds into an ending that gives Kenny — the character who dies constantly — an actual emotional payoff. I never expected a South Park movie to make me feel something, and there I was in the theater, a little moved. Ridiculous, but true.

What impresses me most on rewatch is how tight it is. Barely eighty minutes, no fat, every joke and musical number serving the story. The animation is deliberately cheap, but the writing is anything but — gags come so fast and from so many directions (the V-chip, the MPAA jabs, the finale that's somehow both sincere and mocking) that the movie stays a step ahead of you the whole way.

The great irony, of course, is that a film arguing against censorship had to fight the ratings board tooth and nail to get released. But the argument holds up: the kids' real problem was never the swearing, it was the adults too busy pointing fingers to actually parent. That message predates and outlasts every outrage cycle since.

Crude on the surface, razor-sharp underneath. 10/10, and Uncle F***a forever.

Dear Editor,

I am writing to add my voice to the debate about computers and their effect on our daily lives. Some of your readers seem to believe that these machines are pulling us away from exercise, nature, and one another. I understand that worry, but I firmly believe that computers, when used sensibly, do far more good than harm—and I would like to persuade your readers to see them as the remarkable tools they are.

Consider first what a computer puts within reach of every family in this town. A child can explore the Great Barrier Reef or the ruins of ancient Rome without buying a plane ticket. A student struggling with algebra can find patient, clear explanations at any hour. When my classmates and I researched our local history project, we uncovered photographs and newspaper archives that would otherwise have sat untouched in a library basement. My own grandmother, who lives three hundred miles away, now watches my little brother's birthday parties through video calls and no longer feels cut off from our lives. Distance used to separate families; now it need only separate their bodies, not their hearts. Add to this the practical skills—typing, research, hand-eye coordination from interactive games—that employers increasingly expect, and it becomes clear that the computer is not a luxury but a doorway.

Some argue that time spent at a screen is time stolen from fresh air and friendship. But surely the fault lies with our choices, not with the machine. A hammer can build a bookshelf or smash a window; no one blames the hammer. If a person sits indoors all weekend, the solution is not to ban computers but to build better habits around them. Indeed, the same computer that tempts us to stay inside can send us out: my family has used ours to find hiking trails we never knew existed, to check the weather before a picnic, and to learn which birds visit our feeder each spring. The technology did not replace our walk in the park; it improved it.

The same is true of family life. Critics claim computers silence the dinner table, and in homes without rules that can happen. Yet in my house, the computer has sparked more conversations than it has ended: we share funny videos, plan holidays together, and my parents use it to help me with homework they long ago forgot how to do. Screens are only antisocial when we let them be. A family that agrees on sensible limits—an hour after homework, none at the dinner table—soon discovers that the computer, like the television before it, can be a companion to family life rather than its rival.

Of course, I am not asking anyone to live online. Exercise, sunlight, and face-to-face friendship are as necessary as food, and no sensible person should sacrifice them. My point is simply that we should stop treating the computer as the enemy and start treating it as what it is: a tool whose value depends entirely on the hand that guides it. Teach children to balance screen time with fresh air, and they will inherit both technological skill and healthy habits.

I urge your readers, then, not to pull the plug but to take hold of it. Computers will shape the future whether we like it or not; let us shape the way we use them first.

Yours sincerely,
Alex Moreau

# Julia Child's Duck à l'Orange

Duck à l'Orange is the great classic of French cooking, and there is nothing quite so wonderful as a well-roasted duck with a glossy, bittersweet orange sauce. Do not be intimidated—take your time, and remember that a sauce can always be corrected. Bon appétit!

## Ingredients

- One duck, 4½ to 5 pounds, with neck and giblets reserved
- Salt and freshly ground black pepper
- 3 large oranges
- 1 carrot, sliced
- 1 onion, sliced
- 1 tablespoon sugar
- 3 tablespoons red wine vinegar
- 2 cups chicken stock (or duck stock, if you have it)
- 1½ tablespoons cornstarch or arrowroot
- 2 tablespoons unsalted butter
- 2 tablespoons orange liqueur (optional but delightful)

## Serves 4 to 6

## Instructions

**Roasting the duck:** Preheat your oven to 375°F. Remove the giblets and save the liver for another use. Cut off the wing tips and excess fat from the duck's cavity. Truss the duck so it will roast evenly. Then—and this is essential—prick the skin all over with a sharp fork, especially around the thighs and breast. You are piercing only the fat layer, not the meat. Season the cavity and skin generously with salt and pepper.

Place the duck breast-up on a rack in your roasting pan. Roast for about 1½ hours, pouring off the accumulated fat every 20 minutes or so. Do save this fat—it is liquid gold for frying potatoes! The duck is done when the skin is a handsome brown and the legs move easily in their sockets. Remove the duck to a platter and keep it warm while you make the sauce.

**The orange preparation:** While the duck roasts, remove strips of zest from two oranges with a vegetable peeler, avoiding the bitter white pith. Cut the zest into fine juliennes and blanch them in boiling water for 5 minutes; drain and set aside. Squeeze the juice from two oranges—you will need about ½ cup. Peel the third orange, removing all pith, and cut the flesh into neat segments. Set these aside for garnish.

Julia Child's Duck à l'Orange is a classic French dish that's hard to beat - a beautifully roasted duck with a shiny, tangy orange sauce is just wonderful. Don't worry if it seems intimidating, just take your time and remember that you can always adjust the sauce. Bon appétit!

## Ingredients

- 1 duck, about 4½ to 5 pounds, with neck and giblets
- Salt and black pepper
- 3 large oranges
- 1 carrot, sliced
- 1 onion, sliced
- 1 tablespoon sugar
- 3 tablespoons red wine vinegar
- 2 cups chicken or duck stock
- 1½ tablespoons cornstarch or arrowroot
- 2 tablespoons unsalted butter
- 2 tablespoons orange liqueur (optional)

## Serves 4 to 6

## Instructions

**Roasting the duck:** Preheat your oven to 375°F. Get rid of the giblets and save the liver for later. Cut off the wing tips and extra fat from the duck's cavity. Tie the duck up so it roasts evenly. Now, prick the skin all over with a fork, especially around the thighs and breast - just the fat layer, not the meat. Season the cavity and skin with salt and pepper.

Put the duck in a roasting pan, breast-up, on a rack. Roast for about 1½ hours, pouring off the fat every 20 minutes or so. Save this fat - it's great for frying potatoes! The duck is done when the skin is brown and the legs move easily. Remove the duck to a platter and keep it warm.

**The orange preparation:** While the duck roasts, peel strips of zest from two oranges and cut them into fine strips. Blanch them in boiling water for 5 minutes, then drain and set aside. Squeeze the juice from two oranges - you'll need about ½ cup. Peel the third orange and cut it into segments.

**The sauce:** Pour out the fat from the roasting pan, add the sliced carrot and onion, and brown them lightly. Deglaze with a bit of stock, scraping up the browned juices - that's where the flavor is! Strain the liquid into a saucepan and add the rest of the stock, simmering to reduce a bit.

Make your caramel: boil the sugar and vinegar until it's a deep brown and smells like caramel. Pour in the orange juice - be careful, it will sputter! Then stir the mixture into your sauce.

Blend the cornstarch with a bit of cold water and whisk it into the sauce. Simmer until it thickens, then off the heat, swirl in the butter and liqueur (if using). Add the blanched zest and taste, adjust the seasoning as needed. It should be a balance of sweet, bitter, and tart.

**To serve:** Carve the duck, remove the legs and slice the breast meat. Arrange the meat on a platter, scatter the orange segments around it, and spoon some sauce over the duck. Serve the rest of the sauce on the side, with rice or potatoes and a salad.

If the duck skin has lost its crispness, put it under the broiler for a minute or two - watch it closely! Enjoy with a good Burgundy.

The morning light costs nothing, slipping through
the crack in curtains frayed to cobweb lace,
and I have learned to wear my hours loose,
unbuttoned at the collar, free of chase.

No alarm but the sparrow's liquid call,
no commute but the path to where tomatoes
climb their twine in the communal lot,
where earthworms write their glistening sonatas
beneath the mulch I turned with borrowed tools.
My neighbor saves me seeds in envelopes
labeled in her shaky hand: *Brandywine,*
*Black Krim, the ones that taste of August.*
We trade in currencies the world neglects—
a jar of pickled beets, a laying hen,
the recipe for bread that needs no yeast,
just time, which I possess in bright abundance,
though bankers call it poverty, this slow
accumulation of unhurried days.

My furniture arrives by stranger's truck,
curbside offerings of departed souls
or families upgrading to the new.
Each scratch a story, each water ring
a record of celebrations I inherit
without the debt of ownership that binds
the wealthy to their white-glove anxiety.
The oak table wobbles till I fold
a matchbook under its declining foot—
a solution costing half a cent,
a triumph of improvisation learned
from grandmothers who stretched a chicken
through Wednesday, made the clothesline sing
with sheets like captured clouds, who understood
that enough is not a place you reach
but a way of breathing in the room
you've been given, however small,
however drafty, however cracked.

I walk to the library where worlds await
no down payment, no subscription's monthly bleed,
where the librarian knows my name,
remembers I prefer mysteries in winter,
poetry when the lilacs start their brief
ambitious blooming. Here I am rich
in voices, centuries of whispered thought
pressed to my ear like a seashell's roar
of distant, possible, imagined seas.

The bicycle I found at the church sale,
seventeen dollars, basket rusted sweet,
carries me past windows where the warm
unaffordable glow of restaurant life
frames couples knife-and-forking their way
through conversations about quarterly returns.
I pedal home to lentils simmering
with the last of summer's basil, to bread
I kneaded while listening to rain,
the radio playing something classical,
static and all, because the dial's stuck,
and why fix what still functions, still delivers
Mozart through the hiss like a message
from another century's own poor,
who understood this too: that joy
is not purchased in the end, but made,
stitched from what others discard as worthless,
the too-ripe peach, the overgrown zucchini,
the friendship with the man who repairs
what breaks instead of recommending replacement.

My children, grown now, phone from cities
where rent consumes their optimistic hours,
and I hear in their voices the beginnings
of understanding, the slow dawning
that their childhood was not deprivation
but something we built together from
the material of attention, of presence,
of being unhurried enough to notice
the heron's prehistoric grace at the pond,
the way dough rises like a slow promise,
the worth of a body of water you cannot own
but only visit, only witness, only love
without the deed, the title, the lock.

At evening I sit on the porch I patched
from lumber the storm made free,
watching bats begin their invisible
harvest above the meadow I don't possess
but walk through, weekly, with the dog
who found me, starving, grateful, mine
not by purchase but by mutual need.
The stars emerge like scattered salt,
too numerous to count, too bright to value,
and I feel what I have always felt
in moments of honest stillness: full,
absurdly, lavishly, completely full,
as if the universe were not a store
but a garden, and I a root, a leaf,
a temporary, necessary, singing thing,
participating in the green exuberance
that costs nothing, that asks only
the devotion of a poor woman's
unencumbered, unbegrudging, blooming heart.

Based on the real-life case of Gerry Conlon and the Guildford Four, the film refuses the easy comforts of inspirational biopic conventions, instead immersing viewers in the suffocating nightmare of a justice system that has already decided your guilt before you enter the courtroom.

Daniel Day-Lewis delivers what might be his most physically and emotionally raw performance as Gerry Conlon, a petty Belfast thief whose life careens from minor criminal hijinks in 1970s London to becoming the centerpiece of one of Britain's most notorious miscarriages of justice. The early scenes establish Conlon as almost recklessly charming, a young man whose fundamental decency is obscured by his restlessness and poor judgment. Day-Lewis allows us to see the boy beneath the bluster, making his subsequent transformation all the more shattering. When Gerry and his friend Paul Hill are arrested for the Guildford pub bombings—IRA attacks they had nothing to do with—the film enters a darker register that it never truly abandons.

The interrogation sequences are masterpieces of escalating dread. What elevates "In the Name of the Father" beyond standard issue-issue cinema is Sheridan's refusal to simplify. Trevor Jones's score, with its keening Irish instrumentation, and Peter Biziou's grainy cinematography create an atmosphere of sustained mournfulness. She witnesses repeated patterns: resource extraction disguised as development, environmental protections waived for "national unity," promises of infrastructure investment that never materialize. Her turning point arrives gradually. The political crisis accelerates when climate-induced drought devastates the interior wheat belt. Federal emergency protocols centralize water distribution under military authority. What separation offers, she argues, is scale. A manageable terrain for accountability. The possibility that representatives might live among consequences. The disruption of accumulated pathologies too large and too entrenched for internal reform. She describes attending village assemblies where water distribution is debated, imperfectly but visibly, by people who will pump what they allocate. text:
**Typical scenario:** After completing your PhD you draft a multi‑million‑euro proposal together with several university partners. The project is funded; you become the project manager, while the professor serves as project leader, official applicant, and principal investigator. He attends the regular research‑alliance meetings but does not micromanage the staff, PhD students, etc. He also encourages the project leader to pursue tenure and to write a habilitation thesis.  

**The problem I see:** A tenure‑seeking researcher must demonstrate autonomy. It is common—though not mandatory—for post‑docs to spend one to two years away from their PhD supervisor, either in another research group or in industry, before returning to lead a sub‑team. This pattern is viewed favorably by professorship committees, and many senior academics have followed it. In Germany today the junior‑professorship route exists both with and without a tenure track, yet the habilitation—still often carried out under a senior professor—remains common.  

**How can you showcase your independence?** Should you push hard for the right to publish work on your own, listing the professor merely as a co‑author, even though he neither conceived the experiments nor substantially contributed to the manuscript (perhaps only reviewing it internally before submission)? Must you stress that future competition with junior‑professors will require a record of autonomous publications, even though you are not the official principal investigator but are doing roughly 95 % of the work that secures funding and runs the project?  

This is a delicate conversation because you owe a great deal to the professor who supervised your PhD, yet he also benefits financially from your contributions. Ethically, you recognize that his involvement as a co‑author is limited to attending meetings and occasional manuscript checks. While this arrangement is typical in experimental sciences—where you often rely on the professor’s expensive laboratory equipment—recently introduced junior‑professorships have shifted expectations compared to a decade ago, when the habilitation was the sole path to a professorship under a tenured mentor.  

One possible compromise is to focus more on theoretical papers, where sole authorship is more acceptable and easier to negotiate with the professor. This could allow you to build a stronger, independent publication record while still respecting the collaborative nature of the experimental work.

I think I have a fairly clear grasp of the relationship between ontology and the “logical syntax” of language as presented by Wittgenstein in the *Tractatus*. He posits the existence of atomic entities—mysterious, simple, unaltered objects about which he offers no examples (thesis 2.0211). For the sake of brevity I will refer to this class of objects as **W‑objects**. At the linguistic level, W‑objects correspond exclusively to names (thesis 3.221), and each is assigned a particular logical type (thesis 2.0123).  

Wittgenstein also speaks of *states of affairs*, i.e., configurations of W‑objects. In language these correspond to elementary propositions—configurations of names (thesis 3.21). Beyond these are propositions that are truth‑functions (in the sense of classical propositional calculus) of elementary propositions. This constitutes the pictorial theory of language.

There are, of course, numerous subtleties in the Tractatus’s account of logical form and its ontological implications—issues that are especially intriguing to anyone trained in mathematical logic and formal ontologies. Here, however, I am concerned with the more mystical aspect of the work, which most readers find most puzzling.

To motivate my question, note that Wittgenstein was influenced by Schopenhauer, who—following Kant—held that the will is a thing‑in‑itself. Traces of this influence appear in the solipsistic passages of the *Tractatus* (5.62–5.6331) and in thesis 6.43. Wittgenstein was also indebted to G. E. Moore, whose *Principia Ethica* argues that the good is a simple, unaltered entity. Yet in the *Tractatus* the good does not seem to be treated as a W‑object, despite thesis 6.4, which leaves the statement unexplained.

*Edit:* By “A is an example of a W‑object” I mean roughly that there exists a propositional function f(x) with one free variable, belonging to the perfect language Wittgenstein describes, such that substituting A for x yields a legitimate sentence f(A); equivalently, A occurs as a name in some sentence of that perfect language.  

*Further edit:* In response to Conifold’s remarks on the relation between logical positivism and the *Tractatus*: twentieth‑century philosophy saw a vigorous debate between metaphysical and positivist readings of the work, each supported by serious arguments. Regardless of how that debate is resolved, my interest lies in the following question.

text:
Please let us know of any studies that compare the features of concept mapping with outlining. Many investigations have reported that both outlining and concept mapping are useful for learning and assessment, but they have treated the two methods as black boxes. On the one hand, although outlining has been around longer, there are far more studies indicating that concept mapping is effective for learning and assessment. On the other hand, outlining is more widely used by students and researchers. So, what features differentiate the two approaches? Are there specific characteristics that are advantageous for certain applications but not others?  

Here is what we already know. Miyatsu et al. [1] define the following procedure for outlining: (1) read the entire original passage; (2) keep in mind how the author structures ideas; (3) identify the main ideas; (4) arrange those main ideas in an outline; and (5) use the outline as a cue to retrieve information. These steps closely resemble the procedure advised by Novak and Cañas [2, 3] for designing a good concept map. In particular, steps three and four of the outlining process correspond to the “progressive differentiation” and “integrative reconciliation” processes described in Ausubel’s assimilation theory [4], which form the theoretical basis of concept mapping.  

Mayer [5] found that outlines function as “advance organizers” that facilitate “bridging”—the cognitive process of linking new knowledge to what learners already know [1]. This bridging leads to meaningful learning, a benefit that has been shown to be enhanced through concept mapping [2].  

Lehman et al. [6] compared outlining with concept mapping and reported no statistically significant differences, although the data tended to favor greater improvements in the mapping condition. Bui and McDaniel [7] contrasted skeletal outlines with illustrative diagrams in tasks measuring free recall and short‑answer performance. Both formats improved free recall relative to a control, but illustrative diagrams produced significantly higher short‑answer scores, especially for low‑ability learners. Thus, free recall may be insensitive to how information is organized or visualized, whereas short‑answer performance benefits from richer visual representations.  

Kiewra [8] compared matrices with outlines for handling comparative information. The matrix format provides visual cues that enable users to establish relationships among categories—connections that outlines often overlook. Hansell [9] introduced “post‑organizers” or “arrays,” which combine words, lines, and arrows in a manner similar to concept maps. These tools significantly improved students’ ability to outline by emphasizing the identification of relevant ideas and their integration into a coherent pattern. Consequently, visualizing information appears to play a major role in promoting deeper processing.  

**References**  
1. Miyatsu, T., Nguyen, K., & McDaniel, M. A. (2018). Five popular study strategies: Their pitfalls and optimal implementations. *Perspectives on Psychological Science, 13*(3), 390‑407.  
2. Novak, J. D., & Cañas, A. J. (2008). The theory underlying concept maps and how to construct and use them.

When science denialists claim that something is “just a theory,” they are often harshly rebuked. Most science educators—teachers, journalists, essayists, and the like—agree that the word *theory* carries a strong requirement. For example, Berkeley defines a scientific theory as “a theory … must be strongly supported by many different lines of evidence.” The Smithsonian calls a theory “a well‑substantiated explanation of an aspect of the natural world that can incorporate laws, hypotheses, and facts.” Wikipedia adds that a theory “is well‑supported by many independent strands of evidence, rather than a single foundation.”

Physicists, however, often use the term differently. Dr. Luboš Motl describes a theory as “a detailed and cohesive explanation, even if it only applies to gedanken worlds (thought experiments that don’t match the real universe).” On Physics .SE, users note that for something to be called a “law” there must (or at least should) be experimental evidence, but there is no such requirement for a “theory.” They also point out that an open‑ended research program in which new fundamental papers can be published is routinely termed a “theory.”

Thus, in science the word *theory* can refer either to a well‑supported explanation or to a more speculative hypothesis. The latter may be mathematically sophisticated and reproduce many known properties of the universe, yet lack experimental or observational confirmation that would elevate it above the status quo. If respected scientists do not uniformly treat “theory” as “well‑supported,” why should anyone else? Why should the public accept a definition that contradicts the usage of many scientists, when the scientists themselves seem free to define the term as they wish?

Is this discrepancy limited to physics, or do other scientific disciplines also employ “theory” in this looser sense? We cannot easily compel physicists to change their terminology, so should we admonish educators for ignoring these exceptions? As it stands, they are presenting a misleading picture to the public.

*Edit 2:* This question concerns inconsistent terminology. If one group of scientists defined “planet” as “a gravitationally rounded body that has cleared its orbital zone,” while another used the archaic meaning “wandering light in the sky,” scientific communication would break down. Consequently, astronomers have spent considerable effort agreeing on a single definition for scientific discourse (whether that definition is optimal is a separate matter). Accurate communication among scientists requires shared definitions, even if laypeople retain their own usages. An unresolved disagreement about the meaning of “theory,” documented here with references, suggests a need to explore how scientists themselves use the word.

text:
I think I’ve noticed several conceptual overlaps between Buddhism and Western philosophy and science. What are good sources for comparing and contrasting Western ideas with Buddhism? Which Western works are thought to have been influenced by Eastern thought? Below I list a few speculated commonalities, based on my admittedly incomplete understanding. My knowledge of Buddhism comes mainly from the books of Thích Nhất Hạnh and Alan Watts, and from attending Pure‑Land services for a time.  

**PSYCHOLOGY**  
For example, mindfulness shares some affinities with cognitive‑behavioral therapy (CBT) and with metacognition. Mindfulness involves awareness of one’s thoughts; metacognition adds the ability to monitor and regulate those thoughts. In other words, thinking is not just a random firing of neurons to which we are oblivious. The Buddhist “second noble truth” links suffering to delusion, while CBT attributes emotional suffering to “cognitive distortions.” These distortions typically consist of a lack of present‑mindedness, fixation on the past or future, and a failure to consider events within their full context.  

**LITERATURE**  
When Hamlet asks Rosencrantz and Guildenstern why they would volunteer to go to a prison, they reply that they do not think of Denmark as a prison. Hamlet responds, “[T]here is nothing good or bad, but thinking makes it so.” Here “good” and “bad” refer to pleasure and pain and the degree to which they are experienced. CBT makes a similar claim: emotional suffering arises from the way we think about experiences rather than from the experiences themselves. Buddhism likewise attributes suffering to various delusions, and CBT labels the responsible mental habits “cognitive distortions.”  

In *The Picture of Dorian Gray*, Oscar Wilde writes, “To become a spectator of one’s own life is to escape the suffering of life.” One can be self‑aware in a third‑person sense, or in the first‑person sense of an “I.” Wilde seems to be linking a reduction of suffering to a diminishment of ego. Shortly before writing the novel he penned the foreword to a friend’s book on the *Tao Te Ching*, suggesting that his remark also touches on mindful self‑awareness—the capacity to remain present amid misfortune without being emotionally tormented.  

William Blake’s poem “The Human Form Divine” appears to echo the Buddhist notion of “blessed human existence.” His famous lines—“To see a world in a grain of sand / And a heaven in a wild flower / Hold infinity in the palm of your hand / And eternity in an hour”—evoke a sense of timelessness. Blake was evidently familiar with Vedic material, as discussed in *Awakenings: Blake and the Buddha*.  

**PHILOSOPHY / EPISTEMOLOGY**  
More significantly, Aristotle’s *Nicomachean Ethics* approaches morality by emphasizing character development rather than merely evaluating isolated actions. According to Aristotle, doing the right thing for the wrong reason makes one less ethical than the ideal. Western philosophy groups such approaches under virtue ethics. Both Aristotle and the Buddha can be placed within this tradition, since each stresses the cultivation of wholesome character as the foundation of ethical life.

text:
I became the tech lead of a startup a few months ago. In the org chart, software development sits under Product. Even by startup standards, the codebase I inherited is terrible. For example, the dev team spent three weeks trying to change the static footer text, and even then they only managed to update about 80 % of the pages. When they attempted to modify the footer’s reusable component, several templates broke and nobody could explain why, despite months of working with the code. The original contractors are long gone and left no documentation.  

I have secured buy‑in to clean up the mess, write down what we learn, and reduce technical debt, but first we have to deliver a new medium‑sized feature that touches the whole stack. We know this feature is a stepping stone toward larger initiatives. The codebase is littered with abandoned, half‑finished features, so I got agreement for one developer to spend five days exploring the code and proposing alternative approaches instead of jumping on the first idea that comes up.  

On day three, the product manager asked the developer for an update. The short answer was: “Here are a few ideas, but I don’t know which are viable because the code is a nightmare; we also dealt with a site outage on day two, so I need more time.” That evening the manager scrapped the spike and replaced it with a “prototype” based on one of the suggestions. In doing so, the product manager made several technical decisions on the spot, effectively pulling rank over me as tech lead.  

From this and other incidents I’m convinced the prototype will soon be pushed to production after a quick “does this look OK on your MacBook?” test. I understand the “agile startup” mentality—the willingness to take risk and ship something, anything, to users as quickly as possible. I don’t mind having my authority challenged, but I was explicitly told, “We’re a startup; we’re not into research.” “Research” was treated like a dirty word.  

I can see why the codebase looks the way it does: the product suffers because the processes—and perhaps the culture—are broken. From the trenches, this feels like the worst‑case interpretation of “agile”: make it up as you go, and treat learning from mistakes as a failure. How can I convince the manager that some planning and forethought add value? Or should I simply accept that this is how an “agile startup” is supposed to operate?

We inhabit a jungle devoid of metal and stone, a vast network of giant vines suspended high above everything else. Our existence is intricately tied to the plant life, which supplies all our needs. With heat and drying, they become the most sturdy substance known to our people. Although difficult to sharpen, they make excellent spears, albeit a bit rigid for bow shafts. A significant disadvantage is that they are highly susceptible to water, losing their shape quickly if not protected.
* **Cinder Moss**: This unusual moss glows red and green in the dark and is remarkably resistant to fire. It's a necessity for shielding fires and provides decent illumination. Additionally, it's great for retaining heat during long travels without fire, keeping a person warm for 3-4 days. However, it requires regular maintenance, as it must be kept moist and warm to survive. When it dies, it turns into a powder that loses its previous properties. We soak it in boiling water every few weeks to maintain its vitality. The powder, although causing itching, is useful for masking scents.

Assumptions in place:

We're gradually accumulating supplies from the local areas, but it will take a long time to gather enough material for our own people. Animal bones are available, but those found in the high canopy are often hollow or lightweight, lacking robustness. We're open to using chemical warfare if necessary, but it can be challenging to control and may have unintended consequences, such as rendering food inedible.

I’m working on a WinForms project that deals with 3‑D models, OpenGL graphics, hierarchical project files, and an MVP architecture. The forge therefore saves time, not money.

The forge itself would supply the magical energy needed to fuel the multiple spell copies required to create several items simultaneously, tapping into the planet’s leylines. This process is already established in the setting’s lore: one of the races uses it as a means of sustaining their addiction to magic. The rules for creating magic items, despite their shortcomings, exist and can serve as guidelines whenever the DM needs ideas for custom items.

What I haven’t found are rules for creating magical locations. In the fiction such places are abundant—an island that shifts its position, a mage’s tower brimming with effects that boost its owner’s powers, a ever‑growing magical city‑tree that grants immortality to its planters, floating magical cities, and so on. These are usually fashioned—again, in‑world—by ordinary spellcasters with enough time, material, and power, not by epic mages with dozens of levels. They are the work of 15th‑ to 17th‑level characters, far from godhood but still possessing a substantial amount of power.

text:
Reasoning in mathematics is straightforward and amenable to automation because every mathematical notion—whether it is an integer, a real number, a derivative, an integral, a differential equation, or its solution—can be expressed in terms of a very small repertoire of primitive concepts. In a type‑theoretic foundation of mathematics there are essentially only two basic types, *e* (entity) and *t* (Boolean truth), and all other types, notions, and concepts are built from these two. Hence mathematical reasoning is systematic: we know the full content of each concept. Occasionally we invent new concepts (the “poetics of mathematics”), but even then we can translate them, or suitable approximations, into existing concepts that trace back to the first principles. In this sense mathematical concepts are constructed, or at least describable, in a bottom‑up fashion.

By contrast, reasoning about physics or the broader real world—ontology, metaphysics, nature, the social world, the humanities, emotions, mind, etc.—is far more difficult. We can only hypothesise what a concept eventually entails and how it relates to other concepts; we never possess a complete elucidation of its content. Every research programme uncovers new nuances, creates new concepts, merges old ones, and so on, all in a non‑rigorous manner because the underlying “first principles” are unknown. We do not even know which first principles would be appropriate for describing reality.

The semantics of natural language provides a clear illustration of attempts to uncover such principles. For example, the table in *Elements of Formal Semantics* (Edinburgh University Press) shows how each grammatical category can be represented as a derived type built from the two basic types *e* and *t*. If mathematics is to serve as a model of the world, then the requisite first principles already exist; we merely need to express complex notions—such as “happiness according to Aristotle,” “ontology according to Hegel,” “ontology in a British encyclopedia,” or “ontology according to philosopher N.”—in terms of those basic mathematical notions. Of course, well‑defined concepts are rooted in the internal semantics of particular individuals, and only through collective conventions do they become the shared concepts of scientific communities, legal systems, etc.

I recognise that my thoughts may sound naïve, which leads to my real question: **Is there a discipline within philosophy that seeks to formulate the content of every concept using a small set of primitive notions or types (whether those are the familiar mathematical types or something else)?** If so, what are the names of such philosophical fields? What are the common terms and research themes associated with them? I only need keywords and names; I can explore the details on my own.

title: A Book Of Strife In The Form Of The Diary Of An Old Soul January
prompt: Write the body of a poem titled "A Book Of Strife In The Form Of The Diary Of An Old Soul January". Do not repeat the title. Write about 550 words. Output only the text itself, without any commentary.
text:
January 1.
The old year died as I will die: in sleep,
not knowing when the white came down on it.
I wake to a world cancelled and made clean
as any soul that God has walked through fire.
I am the fire, Lord; walk me through myself.

January 3.
They say you answer prayer. I have prayed long
and heard no voice, yet something kept me praying—
a hunger that was half a memory of bread.
Perhaps the hunger is the answer. Perhaps
the aching is your hand against my wall.

January 6.
Epiphany. The magi kneel again
in every painted window, gold in hand.
I have no gold. I bring you my cold fear,
my January of the heart. Take that.
It cost me more than frankincense and myrrh.

January 9.
The young ask what age is like. I do not say
it is a country where the friends have thinned,
where every stair is taller than before.
I say it is a room grown quiet, God,
until a man must listen or go mad.

January 12.
I dreamed last night the house in which I was a boy
was snowed to the chimneys. At the window, my father
stood looking up. No one was in the room
but me. I could have wept, waking. Or knelt.
The dead are not far off who lived so near.

January 15.
Midwinter now, midpoint of the long gray.
Even my doubts are tired of being doubted.
Old sins come visiting like country cousins
who do not know when it is time to leave.
Lord, you must be the host who shows them out.

January 18.
I quarreled with you this morning at the sink,
both hands in water warm as any mercy.
I said: If you are love, why all this dark?
The tap ran on. The cup came clean. No thunder.
Only, some way, my anger washed away.

January 21.
A thaw. The eaves let go their silver teeth.
Under the white the grass is grudging green.
So, soul, take heart: beneath the frozen wrong
something of you remembers being spring,
and waits there, small as seed, against the light.

January 24.
A bird this morning—one—sang three notes, and stopped,
as if ashamed of being heard so soon.
Sing on, small friend. Winter is real, but so
are you. I will believe for both of us
until my own thawed throat remembers how.

January 27.
My hands upon my knees, the old dog breathing,
the fire ticking like an unhurried clock.
I am not frightened at the dark, but curious.
I think death is a door held open wide
by someone who has waited there all along.

January 30.
They say the old grow near to heaven. Some days
I feel only nearer to my own grave earth.
But you, if you are anywhere, are there
in the gap between the two, and know my name
before I call it out across the cold.

January 31.
So closes the first month of the last lap.
The light is longer by an hour now.
I did not die of winter. Neither heart
nor faith nor hope froze, though they came close.
February, come. I am learning to be held.
